newsitem.title: USA: Florida officials checking damage to citrus crop.
newsitem.headline: Florida officials checking damage to citrus crop.

text.p: Florida state agricultural officials were assessing damage to citrus crops following colder-than-expected temperatures this weekend, a state official said.

Terry McElroy, spokesman for the Florida Department of Agriculture, said many growers were taken by surprise as weather forecasts had predicted less-severe temperatures because of anticipated cloud cover over the state.

"It was not anticipated and not expected, but there was a band of cold weather that worked its way down the Florida west coast," McElroy said. "We're trying now to determine what sort of damage has occurred and to what extent."
Agriculture department assessors are in the fields to determine the extent of damage to Florida's citrus crop as well as fruit and vegetable yields.
"We may know something later today, but it may be a day or so before we can quantify it," McElroy said.
Temperatures dipped into the mid-20s through central Florida's citrus-growing belt early Sunday morning, with a small area recording a low of 19 degrees.

Weather forecasters had expected cloud cover to move across the state, protecting the citrus and vegetable crops from a hard freeze. But when the clouds failed to move quickly enough, temperatures remained below the freezing mark for one to eight hours, depending on the location.
Citrus can be damaged when temperatures fall below 27 degrees Fahrenheit for four hours or more.
The state's main grower cooperative, Florida Citrus Mutual, said members were checking groves for damage.
"We are going to see some damage, especially in the specialty fruit varieties remaining on trees," said Bobby McKown, head of Florida Citrus Mutual.

"Under the processed side of the industry, Florida Citrus Mutual estimates there will be a decline in this year's orange juice yield as a result of Sunday morning temperatures but not a significant loss in boxes of fruit," he added.
The loss in yield is caused by ice forming in the fruit.
As of January 12, some 67 percent of Florida's citrus crop was still on the trees.
According to U.S. Agriculture Department forecasts, Florida growers were expected to harvest 220 million boxes of oranges and 59 million boxes of grapefruits.

In the specialty area, Florida growers were expected to harvest 2.5 million boxes of Temple oranges; 3.8 million boxes of tangelos; 150,000 boxes of K-earlies; and six million boxes of tangerines this season, according to previous USDA estimates.
Citrus is Florida's second-largest industry with an annual impact of $8 billion, according to state officials.

In South Florida, where winter fruits and vegetables are raised, growers also reported some damage to green beans, bananas, corn and other crops. Low temperatures were recorded in the low 30s in south Dade County.
